tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (benchmark/index.mts, benny) and the CPU is stated (Apple M3 Max, Node v18.19.0), but the headline Buffer-API rows hand libxml2-wasm pre-encoded UTF-8 bytes while libxmljs2, which also accepts a Buffer (src/xml_document.cc FromXml), is fed a JS string and converts it inside the timed call; the like-for-like String API rows lose to native on the 35 KB and 2.3 MB files. The numbers have been unchanged since commit 9ed22d8 (2023-12-26, v0.1.0), whose build used no optimisation flag at link and an unstated local Emscripten version, not the HEAD flags the record lists, so these are first-party numbers short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/performance.md (ops/s, Apple M3 Max, Node v18.19.0). Like-for-like string input (both bindings parse a JS string): libxml2-wasm String API 120,578 vs libxmljs2 78,688 ops/s on the 780-byte file (1.53x), 6,013 vs 12,414 on 35,562 bytes (0.48x, slower) and 43 vs 50 on 2,337,522 bytes (0.86x, slower). Buffer API rows: 167,479, 17,114 and 62 ops/s, i.e. 2.1x, 1.4x and 1.2x libxmljs2, but the harness gives the Buffer API a pre-read UTF-8 Buffer while libxmljs2 gets the string and pays the UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion in its timed call even though it also accepts a Buffer. Buffer API vs pure-JS parsers fed strings: 2.1x, 3.4x and 3.3x over @rgrove/parse-xml; 3.2x, 6.3x and 3.9x over fast-xml-parser (ratios derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Measured build (numbers unchanged since commit 9ed22d8, 2023-12-26, package v0.1.0): Emscripten, CI pinned EM_VERSION 3.1.44 but the local Apple M3 Max run does not state its version; libxml2 master 30d22be configured through gulpfile.babel.js (emconfigure autogen.sh --without-python --without-http --without-sax1 --without-modules --without-html --without-threads --without-zlib --without-lzma --disable-shared --enable-static, no explicit CFLAGS) and linked with emcc -s MODULARIZE -s ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH -s SINGLE_FILE and no -O level. Current HEAD differs: CFLAGS='-O2' and link flags -O2 -flto --closure 1 (binding/emcc.txt), EM_VERSION 5.0.2. Baseline libxmljs2 ^0.32.0 is a prebuilt native addon bundling libxml2 2.9.9 (vendor/libxml/include/libxml/xmlversion.h), flags not stated. Node.js v18.19.0.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (docs/performance.md, numbers unchanged since 2023-12-26). Harness asymmetry: benchmark/index.mts passes the Buffer API a pre-read UTF-8 Buffer but passes libxmljs2 the JS string, so libxmljs2's timing includes UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion although its fromXml also takes a Buffer; on like-for-like string input libxml2-wasm is faster only on the 780-byte file and slower than native libxmljs2 on the 35 KB (0.48x) and 2.3 MB (0.86x) files. libxml2-wasm calls dispose() on each document while libxmljs2 documents are freed by GC finalizers inside the timed loop. Version gap: the wasm side was built from libxml2 master 30d22be (late 2023) while libxmljs2 0.32.x bundles libxml2 2.9.9, so part of the gain may come from newer libxml2 rather than the binding. The measured build predates the current -O2/-flto/--closure flags (no -O at link then); the local Emscripten version is not stated and libxmljs2 is a prebuilt binary with unstated flags. Single machine, Node 18, no warm-up or iteration policy stated beyond benny defaults. The bundled libxml2 carries its own license (LICENSE.libxml2).

notes: Real wasm binding with public benchmark code, but the headline 2.1x/1.4x/1.2x over native libxmljs2 compares a no-conversion Buffer path against a string path; the fair String-vs-string rows show it slower than native on medium and large documents. Measured build flags (Dec 2023, v0.1.0) differ from the HEAD flags the record cited; metadata checked: MIT wrapper, 54 stars, last commit 2026-10-05, not archived.

tier_reason: The harness is public (mtcute/benchmarks tests_*/ scripts, results.md) with CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 5700U) and Node.js v18.17.1 stated, but the wasm blobs it times are prebuilt files in vendor/wasm with unstated build flags and are not the shipped @mtcute/wasm build; first-party numbers short of A, so C stands.

corrections.claimed_speedup: @mtcute/wasm README: 'Up to 10x faster than pure JS implementations' (no numbers there). mtcute/benchmarks results.md, which times standalone component blobs, 73 KB payload: gunzip libdeflate-wasm 4,981 ops/s vs pako 1,409 (3.5x), Node zlib 3,301 (1.5x) and fast-zlib 3,271 (1.5x); the MB/s column overstates the pako gap (345.6 vs 63.5 MB/s, 5.4x) because the pako and fast-zlib scripts count compressed bytes while the zlib and libdeflate scripts count uncompressed bytes. At 48 B gunzip libdeflate 1,095,136 vs pako 117,917 ops/s (9.3x) and zlib 162,193 (6.8x). Deflate at 73 KB: libdeflate 34.6 MB/s vs pako 10.9 (3.2x) and zlib 16.9 (2.0x); the no-unroll build matching the shipped flags gives 27.3 MB/s (2.5x pako, 1.6x zlib) but is slower than Node zlib at 48 B (1.35 vs 3.07 MB/s), 443 B (9.75 vs 15.79) and 13 KB (43.7 vs 46.0). AES-IGE tgcrypto-wasm 134.9 MB/s encrypt vs @cryptography/aes 57.8 (2.3x); AES-CTR 137.1 vs 87.5 MB/s (1.6x); SHA-1 teeny-sha1-wasm 280.6 vs rusha 137.7 MB/s (2.0x, rusha's timed region also runs an OpenSSL SHA-1 check); SHA-256 lekkit-sha256 223.4 vs pure-JS sha256-uint8array 205.8 MB/s (1.09x) and slower at 48 B (50.4 vs 53.4) (ratios derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Shipped package: packages/wasm/lib/Dockerfile (alpine:3.18.4 with clang16, lld, binaryen) runs lib/Makefile: -target wasm32-unknown-unknown -nostdlib -ffreestanding -mbulk-memory -O3 -flto=full -fno-inline -fno-unroll-loops -fno-stack-protector -Wl,--lto-O3, plus a -msimd128 variant (mtcute-simd.wasm). The benchmarked blobs are prebuilt files in mtcute/benchmarks vendor/wasm; their build flags are not stated (build-vendor.sh only patches node_modules), the README only says the NU variants add -fno-unroll and -fno-inline. Node.js v18.17.1.
corrections.license: MIT; the tgcrypto-derived AES code in packages/wasm/lib/crypto is LGPL-3.0 (COPYING.lesser, per the package README)
corrections.caveats: Benchmarks are by the mtcute authors (mtcute/benchmarks, results on Node 18.17.1, AMD Ryzen 7 5700U, NixOS; repo not updated since 2023) and time standalone component blobs from vendor/wasm (libdeflate, tgcrypto, teeny-sha1, lekkit-sha256), not the published @mtcute/wasm build, whose libdeflate is modified and whose flags (-fno-inline -fno-unroll-loops) match the slower 'no-unroll' rows. Harness inconsistencies: gunzip MB/s for pako and fast-zlib is computed from compressed bytes but for zlib and libdeflate from uncompressed bytes (compare ops/s instead); the deflate scripts pass JS strings to zlib and pako (UTF-8 encoding inside the timed call) but a pre-built Buffer to libdeflate; rusha's SHA-1 timing includes an OpenSSL SHA-1 validation while teeny-sha1's does not. The no-unroll libdeflate deflate is slower than Node's native zlib at 48 B, 443 B and 13 KB and wins only from 73 KB up; fast-zlib beats it on small payloads; wasm-miniz_oxide deflates 2.8x faster than libdeflate at 73 KB (1,397 vs 498 ops/s) at a worse ratio (67.42% vs 64.65%). Native OpenSSL is far faster than the wasm crypto (AES-CTR 1,791 vs 137 MB/s encrypt at 73 KB; SHA-256 1,065 vs 223; OpenSSL-based IGE 507 vs 135) and tgcrypto as a Node addon beats the wasm build (236 vs 135 MB/s IGE); WebCrypto SHA-1 beats teeny-sha1 at 545 KB (578 vs 292 MB/s). SHA-256 in wasm is about level with pure-JS sha256-uint8array. The authors' own conclusion is to prefer native crypto on Node and use wasm elsewhere. libdeflate compression level not stated. The AES code is LGPL-3.0 (weak copyleft) inside an otherwise MIT package.

notes: Numbers match results.md, but the gunzip MB/s ratio vs pako is inflated by a unit mismatch in the harness (ops/s gives 3.5x, not 5.4x), rusha's timing includes an OpenSSL check, and the shipped no-unroll deflate loses to Node's native zlib below 73 KB. Usability changed from mixed to copyable because every part is OSI-licensed (MIT plus LGPL-3.0 AES); revert if the catalog treats LGPL parts as mixed. Metadata checked: 570 stars, last commit 2026-10-07, not archived.

tier_reason: The only baseline comparison is a README table in UneBaguette/blake3.wasm (author of the competing blake3-wasm-rs) with CPU and Node v24 stated but no benchmark script in that repo; awasm-noble's own README numbers (benchmark/1-hashes-ciphers.ts, 2-parallel.ts) have no baseline, so numbers without reproducible methodology: C.

corrections.caveats: The baseline comparison is not in awasm-noble's own README: its Speed section (Apple M4; blake3 1,940 MB/s single-threaded, 11,058 MB/s for 48x1 MB and 6,564 MB/s for 1x100 MB with threads, which is the '6-10 GB/s' headline) lists awasm figures only. awasm-noble ships a comparison harness (benchmark/internal/hashes.ts against node:crypto, hash-wasm, blake3-wasm-rs and @noble/hashes) but publishes no results from it. The third-party table comes from the README of UneBaguette/blake3.wasm (4 stars), whose author maintains the competing blake3-wasm-rs and whose repo holds no benchmark script; it covers only BLAKE3, so gains for other algorithms against @noble/hashes are unconfirmed. In that table blake3-wasm-rs beats single-threaded awasm-noble at every size on the Ryzen 7 5800X and at 32 B, 64 KB and 10 MB on the Apple M4. At 32 B awasm-noble is still 3.75x (M4, 105 vs 28 MB/s) and 3.1x (Ryzen, 34 vs 11 MB/s) faster than @noble/hashes; the large multiples (33x, about 99x) come from the Ryzen run, where @noble/hashes measured about half its M4 speed, and the threaded figures use web-worker threads. No native baseline (Node's OpenSSL has no BLAKE3; the third-party README says its native blake3-napi addon is faster for large inputs). Confidence reflects the second-hand source.

notes: Third-party numbers match the blake3.wasm README exactly, but that source is a competitor's README with no harness and BLAKE3 only; awasm-noble's own benchmarks have no baseline. Metadata checked: MIT, 52 stars, last commit 2026-09-12, not archived, not a fork.
